headline: New Hampshire public colleges to waive tuition for eligible students starting in 2027
dek: The New Hampshire Promise will cover standard tuition for qualifying residents and community-college transfer students, but not every cost of attending college.
body: New Hampshire residents from families earning up to $100,000 a year will be eligible for tuition waivers at the state’s public universities and colleges beginning in fall 2027, under a new program announced by the University System of New Hampshire. The program is aimed at incoming first-year students and certain community-college transfer students, opening another path into the state’s public higher-education system as families face rising college costs.

The New Hampshire Promise covers standard tuition for eligible students at the University of New Hampshire in Durham and Manchester, Plymouth State University, Keene State College and the University of New Hampshire’s College of Professional Studies online program. The [official USNH program page](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) says the benefit is built from federal, state and institutional grant aid and applies to students who qualify for in-state residency.

Eligibility is narrower than the phrase ‘free college’ might suggest. Students must be enrolled full time, pursuing a first undergraduate degree and meet the program’s academic and financial-aid requirements. USNH lists a minimum 2.7 grade-point average from a student’s prior school, submission of the Free Application for Federal Student Aid and total family income of no more than $100,000 with typical assets. Transfer students can qualify after earning an associate degree through the Community College System of New Hampshire.

The program does not require a separate application. Students must apply for admission to a participating USNH institution and complete the FAFSA; the university system says eligible applicants will then be considered automatically as part of their financial-aid offer. Awards will be reviewed annually based on the student’s FAFSA, academic status and full-time enrollment, according to the system’s published guidance.

That distinction matters for families planning a budget. The promise covers standard tuition, while students may still need loans or other aid for fees, books, housing and meals. The [University System of New Hampshire’s eligibility guidance](https://www.usnh.edu/our-institutions/new-hampshire-promise) also says the program does not apply to January or summer courses. The benefit is therefore a reduction of one major expense, not a guarantee that a student’s total cost of attendance will be zero.

New Hampshire Public Radio reported that the revised program is expected to broaden access compared with the previous version. Tania deLuzuriaga, a University of New Hampshire spokesperson, told [NHPR](https://www.nhpr.org/education/2026-10-02/usnh-unh-plymouth-state-keene-state-tuition-waiver-higher-education-newhampshire) the system estimates 29% more of next year’s incoming class will qualify. Under the earlier structure, students had to complete a more complicated federal Pell Grant process before learning whether they were eligible, a hurdle the new FAFSA-based approach is intended to reduce.

The announcement comes as New Hampshire’s public colleges are managing financial pressure. NHPR reported that the system lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget and that UNH cut $17.5 million from its budget, contributing to staff reductions and a hiring freeze while enrollment has also been declining. Kimberly DeRego, the system’s chief enrollment officer, said the institutions will fund the waivers with endowment money and hope the program attracts donors who want to support lower-income students.

For prospective students, the immediate next step is preparation rather than a new application deadline: watch the participating college’s admissions process, complete the FAFSA for the relevant aid year and keep academic records current. The first cohort will not begin until fall 2027, and the system’s rules leave unanswered questions about how many students ultimately enroll, how the endowment-supported financing performs and whether the program changes enrollment patterns across the four campuses and online program. Those results will determine whether the promise becomes a durable affordability tool for New Hampshire families.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire Promise tuition waiver starts fall 2027
seoDescription: New Hampshire’s public colleges will waive standard tuition for eligible residents and community-college transfer students beginning in fall 2027.
